newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: TENNIS-KAROL HINGIS GETS PRIDE, NOT MONEY FROM DAUGHTER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KAROL HINGIS GETS PRIDE, NOT MONEY FROM DAUGHTER.

text.p: When Martina Hingis became the youngest person in the Open era to lift a Grand Slam trophy above her head last week, her parents swelled with pride.
Her mother and coach Melanie could barely control herself, bounding over a courtside barricade protecting players at the Australian Open to embrace tennis's latest teenage millionaire.
Her father, Karol, also beamed with the pride only a parent can know -- but at 5 a.m. (0400 GMT) in front of the television in his living room in a small flat in Kosice, eastern Slovakia.
Though Martina carries his name, he has never been invited to see her play at a grand slam tournament.
But soon after celebrating his daughter's finest moment, Karol's life began to change almost as much as the precocious 16-year-old tennis star's did.
"People are coming, saying how well off I am at the moment, but they are thinking only of the money which my daughter has won," the 40-year-old Hingis told Reuters.
"It is nonsense. I have never, and I will never take a single dollar from my daughter," he said angrily.

Hingis, a groundskeeper at a local tennis club, has become the envy of many locals and the focus of media rumours that he has been spurned by his daughter, who left then-Czechoslovakia in 1987 at age seven with her mother for a new life in Switzerland.
In fact, little has changed in his life since Martina turned professional two years ago and began climbing the rankings to her present perch of world number two.
Karol has rarely managed to see her since she left, the last time being late last year when Martina and Melanie visited the Czech Republic for an exhibition match.
"Isn't this problem big enough already for me, to not be with my child?," he asked. "What would my daughter think about me after all this? I went to see her whenever it was possible for me," he said.
"(But) if they don't invite me, they probably don't want me to be there," he added sullenly.
Confident, cheeky, supremely gifted, Martina Hingis made every match look easy as she stormed through the women's draw to win the Australian Open.
Always close by is Melanie, a former Czechoslovak champion who took charge of training Martina from the age of two.
But Karol is quick to remind people that he helped as much as he could to mould the heir-apparent to the throne of women's tennis where her namesake, Martina Navratilova, once reigned.
"I was an average-level tennis player in Slovakia, as I have been playing tennis for 30 years," he said.
"Unfortunately, Martina's mother has never mentioned this ...but I do not want to discuss it...even though I am a bit sorry for that," he said.
Ironically, Karol's wish to see more of his daughter in person may be fulfilled very soon.
Slovak tennis authorities have chosen Kosice as the site for the first round of this year's Federation Cup match between Slovakia and Switzerland in March.

But Hingis would not say whether he will have to buy a seat for the chance to watch his daughter play. "My child has tennis before her, let us not talk about these things. Why should she deal with all this stupid din?"
